cards.title: The DDD Revival
cards.teaser: DDD turned twenty-three in 2026 and is more relevant than it was at publication. The reason is not nostalgia — it is that the problems DDD addresses have gotten harder: larger systems, more services, more teams, more domain complexity, and now AI systems that need to reason about the business.

runs.text: Note: this chapter is a snapshot, not a forecast. Tool names and community details reflect the state of the field as of mid-2026. The principles are designed to outlast the examples.
Eric Evans published
Domain-Driven Design

in 2003. For most of the following decade, DDD was a niche practice — respected by architects, ignored by most teams, and largely absent from enterprise adoption. That changed around 2014–2015, when the industry's shift toward microservices exposed a gap that DDD was uniquely positioned to fill: how do you decompose a large system into independently deployable services in a way that reflects the business rather than the database schema?
By 2026, the DDD revival has three distinct drivers:

items.text: Microservices demanded strategic design.

Bounded contexts gave teams a principled answer to service decomposition that "one service per table" and "one service per team" could not. The context map gave architects a tool to reason about cross-service relationships.
Event sourcing needed aggregate design.

The aggregate-plus-events model proved to be the natural data structure for event-sourced systems. Teams that adopted event sourcing without DDD repeatedly reinvented the aggregate pattern — usually less well.
AI systems need domain models.

As LLM-based agents are integrated into business workflows in 2025–2026, the question of how to represent business knowledge explicitly — not buried in code, but expressed in a shared model — has become urgent. DDD's ubiquitous language and bounded context map are the closest thing the industry has to a standard for this.

runs.text: The practitioners driving the 2026 DDD community are not the same as the 2003 cohort. Vaughn Vernon (
Implementing DDD
Domain-Driven Design Distilled
, 2016), Alberto Brandolini (Event Storming), and Vlad Khononov (
Learning Domain-Driven Design
, 2021) are the most widely cited voices. Evans himself remains the canonical source, but his role is more as theorist and originator than day-to-day community driver.

The ddd-community.slack.com workspace and the annual Domain-Driven Design Europe conference remain the primary community gathering points. Vlad Khononov's 2021 book is widely recommended as the more accessible entry point for developers new to DDD — it explains the same concepts with clearer practical examples than Evans' original.

DDD was niche in 2003 and is mainstream in 2026 — not because the ideas changed, but because the problems got harder. Microservices needed bounded contexts. Event sourcing needed aggregates. AI systems need explicit domain models. DDD had the vocabulary the industry needed.

cards.title: DDD and Microservices — Bounded Contexts as Service Boundaries
cards.teaser: The most impactful application of DDD in the last decade is not tactical — it is strategic: using bounded contexts to define microservice boundaries. A bounded context is not the same as a microservice, but it is the right unit of analysis for drawing service lines.

runs.text: The industry learned an expensive lesson in the 2015–2020 microservices adoption wave: cutting services along database tables or technical tiers produces systems that are distributed in deployment but monolithic in coupling. Every service needs data from every other service. Every change ripples across service boundaries. The distributed monolith is the canonical anti-pattern.
The DDD principle that resolves this:
bounded contexts define where a model has coherent meaning.

Within a bounded context, a term like "Customer" or "Order" has a specific, agreed-upon definition. Outside that context, the same term may mean something different, or something related but distinct. The context boundary is the natural service boundary because it is the boundary across which the model changes.
Mapping bounded contexts to microservices:

items.text: One context, one service (ideally).

A bounded context should not be split across multiple services, because that reintroduces the coupling the context boundary was designed to eliminate. A service that spans two bounded contexts carries two models and the friction between them.
One service may initially contain multiple contexts.

In a modular monolith, several bounded contexts coexist in a single deployable. Splitting them into separate services is a later evolution, not a starting requirement. DDD does not mandate deployment topology.
Context map relationships become inter-service contracts.

The upstream/downstream relationship of a customer-supplier context map entry becomes an API contract between services. The anticorruption layer (ACL) pattern becomes an explicit translation layer in the consuming service.
Ubiquitous language becomes API vocabulary.
The events and commands published by a service should use the ubiquitous language of its bounded context. An event named
OrderPlaced
from an Order context is clear; an event named
RecordUpdated
from a generic CRUD service is not.

runs.text: The most common microservice decomposition mistake is mapping services to data entities rather than bounded contexts. If your service is named after a database table ("the Customer service", "the Product service") and it is accessed by every other service in the system, you have distributed your database, not decomposed your domain. Ask: what is the bounded context for this service, and who owns the ubiquitous language inside it?

The right unit for drawing microservice lines is the bounded context, not the database table. A bounded context is the scope within which a domain model has consistent meaning — and that is exactly the scope within which a service should operate.

cards.title: DDD with Event Sourcing — the Natural Pairing
cards.teaser: DDD aggregates and event sourcing fit together better than almost any other combination in software architecture. The aggregate produces events; the event store persists them; the aggregate is reconstituted by replaying them. No ORM impedance mismatch. No state loss.

runs.text: Event sourcing stores the full history of state changes as a sequence of events, rather than storing current state only. The current state of an aggregate is derived by replaying its event stream from the beginning — or from a snapshot if the stream is long.
The pairing with DDD works at every layer:

items.text: Aggregates are the event-producing unit.

Every state change is expressed as a domain event raised by the aggregate root. The aggregate does not mutate state directly — it raises events, and its state is applied from those events. This makes the business meaning of every state change explicit.
Events are the canonical record.

In a traditional system, you can ask "what is the current state of Order 42?" In an event-sourced system, you can also ask "how did Order 42 get to this state, and when did each step happen?" The audit trail is not a separate concern — it is the primary data model.
Ubiquitous language lives in the event names.
Event names like
OrderPlaced
PaymentAuthorized
OrderShipped
are the ubiquitous language rendered as past-tense facts. They communicate exactly what the domain expert would say happened.
Bounded context boundaries become event stream boundaries.
Integration events that cross context boundaries are derived from domain events within a context. The event store per context is consistent with the bounded context model.

runs.text: The primary implementations in 2026 — EventStoreDB (formerly Event Store), Axon Framework, and Marten (for .NET) — all use the aggregate-as-event-stream model that maps directly to DDD terminology. Greg Young, who introduced the modern event sourcing pattern, was explicit about this derivation from DDD.

The critical design rule: domain events describe what happened in the past tense, not what to do next. An event named OrderPlaced is correct; an event named PlaceOrder is a command masquerading as an event. Getting this distinction right in naming is the fastest indicator that a team has internalized both DDD and event sourcing.

In event sourcing, you store every state change as an event rather than storing current state. DDD aggregates are the perfect unit for this: the aggregate raises events when something happens, and its state is rebuilt by replaying those events. The ubiquitous language shows up directly in the event names.

cards.title: DDD with CQRS — Write Side Enforces Invariants, Read Side Optimizes Queries
cards.teaser: CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) is a natural complement to DDD: the write side (commands) routes through aggregates that enforce domain invariants, while the read side (queries) uses purpose-built projections optimized for display. Neither side compromises the other.

runs.text: CQRS, popularized by Greg Young and Udi Dahan building on CQS (Command Query Separation) from Bertrand Meyer, separates the model used for writing state from the model used for reading state. In a CQRS system, a command flows through the domain model — the aggregate — where invariants are enforced and domain events are raised. Queries bypass the domain model entirely and read from purpose-built read models (projections, views) optimized for the specific query.
Why this matters for DDD:

items.text: The aggregate is freed from query optimization pressure.

Without CQRS, aggregates are often distorted by query requirements — adding navigation properties, lazy loading, or extra state to support UI needs. With CQRS, the aggregate is designed purely around invariant enforcement.
Read models are explicit and purpose-built.

Each query scenario has a read model shaped for it: a dashboard summary, a search result, a detail view. These are denormalized, pre-joined, and cached — none of which is compatible with the consistency requirements of the write side.
Eventual consistency is made explicit.

The read model is updated by projecting domain events. There is a brief window after a command where the read model has not yet reflected the new state. CQRS forces teams to reason about and design for this rather than hiding it.

runs.text: CQRS is most often combined with event sourcing in DDD systems (the pattern is commonly called "event sourced CQRS" or "ES+CQRS"), but the two are independent. You can have CQRS with a traditional relational write model. You can have event sourcing without CQRS. The combination is simply common because they solve complementary problems.

CQRS is not appropriate for every system. Udi Dahan's guidance has always been to apply it selectively: use it for the core domain where complexity justifies the overhead; use simple CRUD for supporting and generic subdomains where the write and read models are essentially the same. Applying CQRS everywhere produces accidental complexity that defeats its purpose.

CQRS means you have two separate models: a write model (the aggregate, which enforces business rules) and a read model (a projection, which is optimized for the screen or report). Queries never touch the aggregate. Commands never touch the projection. Each side is designed for its job.

cards.title: Modular Monoliths and DDD — DDD Doesn't Require Microservices
cards.teaser: DDD's strategic patterns work inside a single deployable as well as across a network. The modular monolith — a single process with strict module boundaries enforced by the build — is a DDD-aligned architecture that avoids distributed systems complexity while preserving the ability to extract services later.

runs.text: The microservices era introduced a false equivalence: DDD = microservices. This mistake is expensive. Teams that decompose systems into microservices before the domain model is stable are breaking apart a model they do not yet understand — and the cost of cross-service changes in a distributed system is much higher than the cost of module changes in a monolith.
The modular monolith restores the correct relationship: bounded contexts are the primary design unit; deployment topology is a later, separate decision. In a modular monolith:

items.text: Each bounded context is a module with a strict public API.
No direct access to another module's internal types, repositories, or database tables. The module boundary enforces the context boundary.
Cross-context communication is explicit.

Modules communicate via published interfaces and domain events — the same contracts they would publish if they were separate services. This makes extraction to a microservice a deployment decision, not a refactoring event.
Build tooling enforces the boundaries.

Tools like ArchUnit (Java/Kotlin), NDepend (.NET), and Module Boundaries rules in NX (Node.js monorepos) reject builds that contain illegal cross-module dependencies. The boundary is not a convention — it is a constraint.
One database, separate schemas or separate tables.

A modular monolith typically shares one database process but uses separate schemas per bounded context (or at minimum, avoids cross-schema joins). This maintains data isolation while avoiding the operational complexity of distributed transactions.

runs.text: The recommendation from practitioners including Sam Newman (
Building Microservices
, 2nd ed.) and Vlad Khononov (
Learning Domain-Driven Design

) converges on a common starting point: build a well-structured monolith first. Extract services when there is a specific operational or scaling driver. The modular monolith is not a compromise — it is the right starting architecture for most systems.

The modular monolith pattern was popularized in the Rails ecosystem by the Packwerk gem (Shopify) and in Java by Moduliths (Spring). In 2026 it is a mainstream architectural recommendation, not an edge case. The shift is a correction from the microservices-first default of 2015–2020.

DDD gives you bounded contexts regardless of whether you deploy as one process or fifty. A modular monolith applies DDD's strategic patterns — strict module boundaries, separate models per context, no cross-context internal access — while keeping everything in one deployable. Extract to microservices later if and when you have a reason.

cards.title: ACL for Legacy Migration — Protecting the New Model
cards.teaser: When migrating from a legacy system, the anticorruption layer (ACL) is the tool that prevents the old model's concepts from contaminating the new domain model. Without an ACL, the legacy data structure gradually reshapes the new model to match the old one.

runs.text: Legacy migration is the most common context in which DDD is applied in 2026. Most organizations are not building greenfield systems — they are replacing, extending, or wrapping systems built in the 2000s and 2010s that carry the technical and conceptual debt of their era.

The anticorruption layer (ACL) — introduced by Evans in the original DDD book — is a translation layer that converts the legacy system's model to the new bounded context's model. Without it, the new system conforms to the legacy model: field names, data structures, and domain concepts from the old system leak into the new one.
ACL migration pattern in practice:

items.text: The ACL lives at the boundary.
It is the only code that knows about both the legacy model and the new model. Everything inside the new bounded context uses only the new model's ubiquitous language.
The ACL is an explicit domain service or adapter.
It is not a mapper buried inside a repository. It is a named, tested component with a clear responsibility: translate from the legacy world to the new world.
Strangler Fig + ACL is the standard migration pattern.

Martin Fowler's Strangler Fig pattern (incrementally replace legacy functionality) combined with an ACL is the industry-standard approach: new features use the new model; the ACL translates when the new model needs data from the legacy system; the ACL shrinks as legacy capabilities are migrated.
The ACL reveals model impedance.

Complex ACL translation code is a signal: the two models are conceptually different. Trivial ACL translation (mostly field renaming) suggests the old model was not as wrong as assumed. The complexity of the ACL is diagnostic.

runs.text: The Open Host Service (OHS) pattern is the ACL's counterpart: where the ACL protects the consumer, the OHS protects the producer. A legacy system that publishes a clean, versioned API for consumers to integrate against is acting as an OHS — even if the implementation is legacy code.

The most common ACL failure: the translation layer grows into a general-purpose integration service that both new and old code depend on, collapsing the boundary it was designed to enforce. Keep the ACL strictly one-directional: legacy model in, new model out. Never let new-model concepts flow back through the ACL into legacy code.

When you're replacing a legacy system, the ACL is the firewall between the old model and the new one. It translates legacy data structures into your new domain model's language so that the legacy system's bad concepts don't infect the new code.

cards.title: Vernon's Red Book — Implementing DDD as the Practical Companion
cards.teaser: Vaughn Vernon's Implementing DDD (2013) is the book that made DDD practitioner-accessible. Where Evans wrote for architects reasoning about design, Vernon wrote for developers writing code. The red book remains the most recommended DDD book for engineers new to the discipline in 2026.

runs.text: Eric Evans'
Domain-Driven Design

(2003) — the "blue book" — is the canonical source. It is also a difficult book: abstract in places, meander-heavy, and not organized around how a developer would approach implementing a system. For years, a significant barrier to DDD adoption was the gap between understanding the concepts and knowing how to apply them in code.
Vaughn Vernon's
Implementing Domain-Driven Design

(2013) — universally called the "red book" — bridges that gap. It works through every major DDD pattern with concrete Java examples, explicit implementation guidance, and worked examples of how patterns interact. The red book covers:

items.text: Bounded contexts and context maps with implementation examples.
Not just what they are, but how to structure Java packages, define interfaces between contexts, and enforce boundaries in code.
Aggregates with explicit design rules.
Vernon's "four rules of thumb" for aggregate design — small aggregates, reference by ID, eventual consistency between aggregates, one transaction per aggregate — are now standard guidance.
Domain events with publish-subscribe infrastructure.
The red book provides concrete patterns for raising, dispatching, and handling domain events that influenced event sourcing implementations.
CQRS and event sourcing integration.
Vernon's coverage of CQRS and event sourcing in the context of DDD was the first widely-read treatment of how these patterns combine — predating most of the microservices era enthusiasm.

runs.text: Vernon followed the red book with
Domain-Driven Design Distilled
(2016), a shorter, more accessible introduction. In 2026, the reading order most commonly recommended by practitioners is:
DDD Distilled
for orientation,
Learning Domain-Driven Design
(Khononov, 2021) for a modern practical treatment, and the red book as reference. Evans' blue book is respected and cited but rarely recommended as a first read.

Vernon's four aggregate design rules, originally from the red book, have become the default teaching framework for aggregate design: (1) design small aggregates, (2) reference other aggregates by identity only, (3) use eventual consistency for cross-aggregate business rules, (4) one aggregate per transaction. These rules are simple enough to remember and strong enough to prevent most aggregate design errors.

Evans wrote the foundational theory. Vernon wrote the how-to guide. If you want to understand DDD philosophically, start with Evans. If you want to implement it in code next week, start with Vernon's red book or Khononov's Learning DDD.

cards.title: Event-Driven Architecture — DDD's Natural Runtime
cards.teaser: DDD's emphasis on domain events and bounded context integration maps naturally to event-driven architecture (EDA). Events are the medium through which bounded contexts communicate without coupling. In 2026, the event broker is infrastructure; the domain model gives the events their meaning.

runs.text: Event-driven architecture uses asynchronous events as the primary integration mechanism between components. Bounded contexts produce events when their state changes; other bounded contexts subscribe to and react to those events. The producing context does not know or care which other contexts consume its events.
Why DDD and EDA are natural partners:

items.text: Bounded context autonomy.

In a synchronous, request-response integration, the producing context must be available when the consuming context needs data. In an event-driven integration, the contexts are temporally decoupled. This aligns with the DDD principle that contexts should be independently evolvable.
Integration events vs domain events.

Domain events are raised internally within a bounded context for internal coordination. Integration events are the subset published to the event bus for other contexts to consume. The DDD distinction keeps internal domain events from leaking their internal model to external contexts.
Events as the published language.
The event schema published to the bus is an Open Host Service (OHS) with the event bus as the transport. Versioning these schemas requires the same rigor as versioning a REST API.
Event brokers are infrastructure, not domain.

Kafka, RabbitMQ, AWS EventBridge, and Azure Service Bus are delivery mechanisms. The bounded context and its domain model are independent of the broker choice. An event-driven DDD system should be able to switch brokers without changing domain code.

runs.text: Patterns that combine EDA and DDD in 2026:

items.text: Saga / process manager for cross-context workflows.

Long-running business processes that span bounded contexts are coordinated via sagas — sequences of events and commands with compensating transactions on failure. The saga is a domain concept (not a technical framework choice), living in its own bounded context.
Outbox pattern for reliable publishing.

Domain events written to an outbox table in the same transaction as the aggregate state change, then relayed to the broker by a background process, guarantee at-least-once delivery without distributed transactions.

runs.text: The most common EDA + DDD failure is publishing the aggregate's internal state as the event payload rather than designing the integration event schema explicitly. When the internal aggregate changes, the published event changes, and every consumer breaks. Design integration events as a separate, stable schema — not a serialized aggregate.

Event-driven architecture and DDD are natural partners: bounded contexts publish domain events to a broker, and other contexts subscribe to them. The contexts are decoupled — the producer does not know or care about its consumers. The event schema is the contract; the domain model is what gives the events their meaning.

cards.title: DDD-Lite — Just the Patterns Subset
cards.teaser: DDD-Lite is the pragmatic subset of DDD that teams adopt without committing to the full methodology: entities, value objects, aggregates, and repositories applied tactically to make the domain model more expressive — without the strategic layer (ubiquitous language, context mapping) that requires organizational commitment.

runs.text: Full DDD is a significant investment. Ubiquitous language requires sustained collaboration with domain experts. Context mapping requires organizational visibility. Event storming requires workshop facilitation. For many teams, particularly those working on supporting subdomains or in organizations where domain expertise is not accessible, the full DDD methodology is not feasible.

DDD-Lite, a term coined informally by the community, refers to the tactical pattern subset: using entities, value objects, aggregates, and repositories to structure domain code without the strategic context. It produces noticeably better domain code than anemic models or service-layer patterns, at a fraction of the organizational cost.
What DDD-Lite includes:

items.text: Rich domain objects.
Entities with behavior, not just data. Value objects replacing primitives. Aggregates enforcing invariants.
Repository pattern.
A collection-like interface over persistence, one per aggregate root.
Domain events (optional).
Explicit events for significant state changes, published internally.

runs.text: What DDD-Lite omits:

items.text: Ubiquitous language as a formal practice.
The code uses meaningful domain names, but there is no explicit process of aligning terminology with domain experts.
Context mapping.
The system-level view of context relationships is not explicitly modeled.
Event Storming and knowledge crunching.
No facilitated workshops; domain knowledge is captured through code review and documentation.

runs.text: The risk of DDD-Lite is that it produces good-looking domain code without the deep model understanding that makes DDD valuable. Aggregates named after database entities, value objects without real domain meaning, and repositories that are DAOs with a different name are DDD-Lite done wrong. The patterns are only as good as the model they encode. Without domain collaboration, the patterns are vocabulary without content.

DDD-Lite is the tactical pattern subset without the full strategic investment: you use entities, value objects, aggregates, and repositories to write better domain code, but you skip the formal ubiquitous language and context mapping work. It is a pragmatic starting point, not the destination.

cards.title: AI-Assisted Domain Modeling
cards.teaser: LLMs can participate in domain modeling activities — drafting ubiquitous glossaries, suggesting aggregate boundaries, transcribing event storming workshops, and identifying missing domain events from requirements. The practice is in early-adopter phase as of 2026. Results are uneven.

runs.text: This card is explicitly marked as an early-days assessment. AI-assisted domain modeling is an active area of experimentation and the state of the art is moving quickly. Treat claims in this card as provisional.
Where AI assistance is showing genuine value in domain modeling work:

items.text: Glossary drafting from documents.

LLMs can extract candidate ubiquitous language terms from requirements documents, user stories, and meeting transcripts. The output requires review by a domain expert but reduces the initial effort significantly. In one published account from Thoughtworks (2025), this cut glossary drafting time by roughly 60% — though the quality review remained manual.
Event storming facilitation support.

LLMs can prompt for missing events ("Have you modeled what happens when the payment fails at step 4?"), identify gaps in command-event-aggregate chains, and suggest candidate hotspots (conflicting models). Alberto Brandolini has noted this use case with cautious interest — the LLM as a "devil's advocate" in the workshop.
Transcription and synthesis.

Workshop recordings transcribed and summarized into event catalogs, draft context maps, and glossary entries. This is the highest-confidence application — the LLM is doing information extraction, not domain reasoning.
Context map suggestions from system descriptions.

Given a description of a system and its subdomain responsibilities, LLMs can propose candidate bounded contexts and context relationships. These are starting hypotheses, not final designs, and should be validated with domain experts.

runs.text: Where AI assistance has produced poor results:

items.text: Deep domain reasoning without expert input.

LLMs trained on generic software examples produce generic domain models. The finance domain "Order" is not the same as the e-commerce "Order." Without domain expert correction, LLMs converge on the most common pattern in training data, not the correct model for the domain.
Aggregate boundary decisions.

Aggregate design requires understanding the domain's consistency requirements, transaction frequency, and invariant structure. LLMs lack access to these constraints and produce structurally plausible but contextually wrong aggregate designs.

runs.text: The most useful frame for AI in domain modeling: LLMs are good at breadth (generating candidate terms, events, contexts) and poor at depth (understanding why a specific aggregate boundary is correct for this domain's consistency requirements). Use them to generate options that a domain expert selects from, not to make modeling decisions.

LLMs can help with the mechanical parts of domain modeling — drafting glossaries, transcribing workshops, suggesting candidate bounded contexts. They cannot replace the domain expert who knows why the Shipping context and the Billing context need different definitions of Customer. As of 2026, AI assists the modeler; it does not replace the modeling conversation.

cards.title: Living Documentation — Keeping Model and Code Aligned
cards.teaser: The biggest DDD failure mode in practice is not bad design — it is design that was correct but was not maintained as the code evolved. Living documentation practices use tooling (Structurizr, C4 Model, context map generators) to keep the architectural model visibly in sync with the code.

runs.text: DDD's core promise is that the code and the domain model are the same thing — the code is the model. In practice, models drift: the context map drawn in the event storming workshop no longer reflects the service landscape after eighteen months of feature development; the glossary in the wiki no longer matches the class names in the codebase; aggregate boundaries documented in ADRs have been quietly violated in implementation.
Living documentation addresses this by generating architectural artifacts from the code, rather than maintaining them separately. Key tools:

items.text: Structurizr.

Simon Brown's Structurizr (structurizr.com) implements the C4 Model (Context, Container, Component, Code) as a workspace that is versioned alongside code. The architecture model is defined in DSL or Java/C#/Python and rendered as diagrams on demand — the diagram is a view of the model, not a standalone artifact that can diverge.
ArchUnit and equivalent build-time checks.

Architecture rules expressed as tests: "no class in the Order context may reference a class in the Billing context directly." If the code violates the rule, the build fails. The documentation of context boundaries is enforced, not advisory.
EventCatalog.

An open-source tool (eventcatalog.dev) that generates event documentation from AsyncAPI and schema definitions. In an event-driven DDD system, the event catalog is the living documentation of the integration events published by each bounded context.
Context map generators.

Context Mapper (contextmapper.org) is a DSL and Eclipse plugin for modeling context maps, generating diagrams, and deriving skeleton service structures from the map. It supports the full set of DDD context map patterns in an executable specification.

runs.text: The discipline principle behind living documentation:
if the documentation can drift from the code, it will.
Every architectural diagram that exists only as a PNG in a Confluence page is a diagram that will be wrong within a year. Make the model executable. Make drift a build failure.

Simon Brown's C4 Model (c4model.com) gives a vocabulary for architectural levels (Context, Containers, Components, Code) that maps cleanly onto DDD strategic and tactical layers. The C4 Context level corresponds to bounded contexts and their relationships; the Container level corresponds to services within a context; the Component level corresponds to aggregates and domain services. It is the most widely adopted architectural documentation vocabulary in the DDD community.

Living documentation means the architectural model is generated from the code, not maintained separately. Tools like Structurizr, ArchUnit, and Context Mapper keep the bounded context diagram, the event catalog, and the architecture rules in sync with the actual codebase — because drift is automatic if you don't build it in.

cards.title: Bounded Contexts for AI Agents — Multi-Agent Systems as Context Maps
cards.teaser: As multi-agent AI systems become common in 2025–2026, the context map pattern finds a new application: modeling the boundaries between AI agents. Each agent has a scope of responsibility, a vocabulary, and explicit interfaces to other agents — the same structure as a bounded context.

runs.text: Multi-agent AI systems — architectures in which multiple specialized language model agents collaborate to complete a task — introduce the same design problem that bounded contexts were invented to solve: how do you define the scope of each agent, what vocabulary does it use, and how do agents communicate without one agent's conceptual model corrupting another's?
The parallel is structural, not superficial:

items.text: Each agent has a bounded context.

Its scope of reasoning, its vocabulary, and its system prompt define the context boundary. An agent responsible for code review has a different model of "change" than an agent responsible for deployment. The same word means different things in each agent's context.
Agent interfaces are context map relationships.

When one agent needs a result from another, the interface — the tool schema or message format — is a context map boundary. The question "is this a customer-supplier or a conformist relationship?" applies as directly to agent interfaces as to service APIs.
ACLs protect agent models.

If a planning agent's output is passed directly to a coding agent, the planning agent's terminology and structure may not match the coding agent's model. A translation layer — an ACL — converts the output of one agent into the vocabulary of the next.
Ubiquitous language in agent system prompts.

Defining terms explicitly in the agent's system prompt — "In this context, 'deployment' means applying a Kubernetes manifest to a cluster, not updating a configuration file" — is ubiquitous language for AI agents.

runs.text: This application of DDD to multi-agent systems is early-stage. As of 2026, the community is actively exploring it — Vaughn Vernon has written about it in online forums, and Vlad Khononov has referenced the parallel in conference talks. It is not yet a formalized pattern with a body of practitioner experience, but the conceptual fit is strong.

Anthropic's guidance on building multi-agent systems ("Building effective agents," 2024) emphasizes clear scope boundaries and minimal, explicit interfaces between agents — advice that reads like a restatement of bounded context principles. Whether or not the DDD vocabulary becomes standard in AI agent design, the underlying problem it solves is the same.

Multi-agent AI systems face the same design problem as microservices: how do you define what each agent is responsible for, what vocabulary it uses, and how it talks to other agents without creating confusion? Bounded contexts, context maps, and ACLs are applicable design tools — the context is AI agents instead of services, but the structure is identical.

cards.title: The DDD 2026 Community
cards.teaser: The DDD community in 2026 is active, practitioner-led, and more diverse than at any prior point. The four names that appear most in practitioner reading lists — Evans, Vernon, Brandolini, Khononov — span four different decades of contribution and four different entry points into the discipline.

runs.text: The DDD community has always been smaller and more practitioner-focused than communities around popular frameworks. In 2026 it is larger than at any prior point, with active conference tracks, a substantial Slack workspace, and a growing body of polyglot examples (beyond the Java-heavy early literature).
The four canonical practitioners:

items.text: Eric Evans.
Author of
Domain-Driven Design

(2003, Addison-Wesley). Co-founder of Domain Language Inc. Evans occupies the role of theorist and originator. His public writing in 2026 focuses on the limits and evolution of DDD — he is notably cautious about overclaiming what DDD can solve and honest about the conditions under which it fails.
Vaughn Vernon.
Author of
Implementing Domain-Driven Design
Domain-Driven Design Distilled

(2016). Founder of Reactica and the vaughnvernon.com body of work. Vernon's contribution is implementation clarity: he takes Evans' concepts and explains how to put them in code. In 2026 he is writing about DDD in functional programming contexts and the multi-agent system parallels.
Alberto Brandolini.
Creator of Event Storming. Author of
Introducing EventStorming

(Leanpub, ongoing). Brandolini's contribution is the modeling workshop — the method for extracting and aligning domain knowledge in collaborative sessions. In 2026 he is exploring AI participation in event storming sessions and the limits of remote-first facilitation.
Vlad Khononov.
Author of
Learning Domain-Driven Design

(O'Reilly, 2021). Khononov's contribution is the modern restatement: he explains DDD with current architectural context (microservices, event-driven systems, bounded context maps), more accessibly than any prior author.
Learning DDD
is the most commonly recommended entry point for developers new to DDD in 2026.

runs.text: Community resources that remain active in 2026: Domain-Driven Design Europe (annual conference, dddeurope.com), ddd-crew on GitHub (community patterns and worksheets), and the Context Mapper open-source project (contextmapper.org) for tooling.

The DDD community's distinguishing characteristic is its resistance to hype cycles. Practitioners are vocal about the conditions under which DDD is overkill, the cost of applying it incorrectly, and the value of simpler designs for non-core domains. This intellectual honesty has given DDD unusual longevity in a field prone to methodological fashion cycles.

Four people define the DDD canon in 2026: Evans wrote the theory, Vernon made it implementable, Brandolini created the workshop method, and Khononov wrote the modern accessible entry point. Start with Khononov's Learning DDD, read Vernon's red book for implementation depth, and consult Evans when you want the original thinking.

cards.title: What's Load-Bearing in DDD — and What Has Aged
cards.teaser: Twenty-three years after the blue book, it is worth separating what has stood the test of scale from what reflects the specific context of 2003. The core strategic patterns remain essential; some tactical details have aged; the organizational and cultural requirements were underestimated.

runs.text: This card is explicitly evaluative and partially speculative. It represents a best-effort practitioner view as of 2026.
Load-bearing — endures across architecture generations:

items.text: Bounded contexts and ubiquitous language.

The most important ideas in DDD. The bounded context is the correct unit for reasoning about model scope, service boundaries, team autonomy, and AI agent design. Ubiquitous language is the correct mechanism for aligning developers and domain experts. These have not aged.
Aggregates as consistency boundaries.
The aggregate pattern — and Vernon's four rules — is the most widely applied DDD tactical pattern and produces measurably better domain models than alternatives.
Context map patterns.
The eight context map relationships (ACL, OHS, conformist, etc.) are as useful for reasoning about microservice relationships as they were for reasoning about monolith boundaries.

runs.text: What has aged or been superseded:

items.text: The factory pattern as described.

Evans' factory treatment reflects 2003-era OOP patterns. Modern DDD implementations use named constructors on aggregates and value objects rather than separate factory classes in most cases. The pattern still exists; the canonical form has been simplified.
The four-layer architecture.

The Domain / Application / Infrastructure / Presentation layer model from the blue book has been largely superseded by hexagonal (ports and adapters) and clean architecture formulations, which make the dependency rule more explicit and do not require a specific layer stack.
The knowledge-crunching process as described.

Evans describes a sustained pair-working process between a developer and a domain expert to build the model. In most 2026 organizations, event storming (Brandolini, 2013) has replaced or supplemented this as the primary knowledge extraction mechanism — it is faster, more collaborative, and scales to larger teams.

runs.text: What was underestimated in the original:

items.text: The organizational requirement.

DDD requires access to domain experts who can engage meaningfully in model conversations. In many organizations, domain experts are not available, not interested, or not trusted with technical design decisions. DDD without domain collaboration produces technically sophisticated models of the wrong thing.
The cost of maintaining the model.

The blue book treats model maintenance as a natural consequence of domain collaboration. In practice, maintaining a living domain model under continuous delivery pressure requires explicit processes and tooling (living documentation, architecture fitness functions). Without them, the model diverges from the code within months.

runs.text: The single best test for whether a DDD implementation is working: can a new team member, after two weeks, explain the system's bounded contexts, name the core aggregates in each, and describe how contexts communicate — without reading the code? If yes, the model is alive. If no, it is documentation.

The strategic patterns — bounded contexts, ubiquitous language, context maps — have aged exceptionally well and are more applied in 2026 than in 2003. Some tactical details and the original four-layer architecture have been refined or superseded. The biggest thing the blue book underestimated: how hard it is to sustain domain collaboration in real organizations, and how fast the model drifts if you don't maintain it actively.
